domains.name: Security, Compliance, and Governance for AI Solutions

questions.stem: A product manager is preparing a slide for executives about AI terms. Which statement correctly describes how AI, machine learning (ML), deep learning, and generative AI relate to each other?

options.text: Generative AI is a subset of deep learning, deep learning is a subset of ML, and ML is a subset of AI
options.why: Each circle sits inside the one before it: AI is the umbrella, ML learns from data, deep learning uses many-layered neural networks, and generative AI is a capability within deep learning.

options.text: ML is a subset of generative AI, and generative AI is a subset of deep learning
options.why: This turns the circles inside out. Generative AI is the newest, narrowest circle, not the umbrella over ML.

options.text: AI and ML are separate fields that do not overlap, and deep learning belongs only to AI
options.why: ML is a branch of AI, so the two always overlap. Every ML system is an AI system.

options.text: Deep learning and generative AI are two names for the same thing
options.why: Deep learning also covers models that only classify or predict, such as spotting defects in photos. Generative AI is the part of deep learning that creates new content.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'relate to each other'. Rule: four circles, biggest to smallest: AI, then ML, then deep learning, then generative AI.

questions.stem: A bank trained a model last month on historical card transactions. The model now scores each new transaction as it arrives. What is this second activity called?

options.why: Training is when the model learns patterns from historical data. That already happened last month.
Labeling means tagging data with the right answer before training. Scoring new transactions doesn't add labels.
Inferencing is using an already trained model to produce an output for new input, which is exactly what scoring each new transaction is.
Feature engineering creates and selects the input variables before training. It isn't the act of making predictions.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'already trained' + 'new transaction'. Rule: training is the model studying; inferencing is the model sitting the exam.

questions.stem: A media company wants to automatically sort millions of unstructured photos and audio clips. A consultant recommends a technique that uses neural networks with many layers. Which technique is the consultant describing?

options.why: Rules-based systems follow instructions a person writes by hand. They don't use neural networks and struggle with messy data like photos.
Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple layers and is especially good at unstructured data such as images, audio and text.
Linear regression predicts a number from a straight-line relationship. It isn't a many-layered neural network.
Reinforcement learning is about learning actions by trial and error with rewards. The 'many layers' hint points to the model's structure, which is deep learning.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'neural networks with many layers' + 'unstructured'. Rule: many layers of artificial neurons = deep learning.

questions.stem: A factory wants a system that looks at camera images of products on a conveyor belt and flags defective parts. Which field of AI does this use case belong to?

options.why: NLP works with human language, such as text and speech. Camera images of parts are visual input.
Speech recognition turns spoken audio into text. There is no audio in this scenario.
Recommendation systems suggest items to users from past behavior. They don't inspect images.
Computer vision lets computers get meaningful information from images and video, and spotting product defects on a line is a classic example.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'camera images'. Rule: if the input is pictures or video, the field is computer vision.

questions.stem: A hotel chain wants software that reads thousands of written guest reviews and works out whether each one is positive or negative. Which field of AI does this describe?

options.why: Understanding the meaning and sentiment of written text is NLP. Amazon Comprehend, for example, uses NLP to find sentiment in documents.
Computer vision works with images and video. Written reviews are text.
Reinforcement learning learns actions from rewards. Reading reviews for sentiment is a language task, not a trial-and-error one.
Forecasting predicts future values from data ordered in time. Sentiment of a review is about the meaning of the words.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'written reviews' + 'positive or negative'. Rule: text meaning, sentiment, entities = NLP.

questions.stem: A travel company wants a system that is given a goal, such as rebooking a customer after a cancelled flight, and then plans the steps, calls booking tools, and acts on its own. Which term describes this kind of system?

options.why: A rules-based chatbot follows a fixed script. It doesn't reason about a goal or choose which tools to call.
Supervised learning is a way to train a model from labeled examples. It describes training, not a system that plans and acts.
Agentic AI is an autonomous system that acts independently toward a goal, using reasoning, memory and tools in a loop of perceive, reason, act and learn.
Batch inference runs a model over a large set of inputs at once. It says how predictions are delivered, not that the system acts on its own.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'given a goal' + 'calls tools' + 'acts on its own'. Rule: a model that only answers is generative AI; one that plans and takes actions is agentic AI.

questions.stem: A sales team is evaluating a writing assistant built on a large language model (LLM). Which statements correctly describe an LLM? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: It is a very large deep learning model pre-trained on vast amounts of data
options.why: That is AWS's own definition of an LLM: a very large deep learning model pre-trained on huge amounts of data.

options.text: It is one class of foundation model
options.why: Foundation models are large models trained on broad data, and LLMs are the class of them that work with language.

options.text: It follows if-then rules that the team writes by hand
options.why: An LLM learns patterns from data. Hand-written if-then rules describe a rules-based system.

options.text: It must be trained from scratch on labeled examples before each new task
options.why: An LLM is pre-trained once and then used for many tasks, often with just a prompt. No per-task labeled training is required.

options.text: It always gives exactly the same answer to the same prompt
options.why: LLM output can vary from run to run because generation involves chance. This is called nondeterminism.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'large language model'. Rule: an LLM is a deep learning model, pre-trained on huge data, and one kind of foundation model.

questions.stem: A retailer's model predicts returns with 98% accuracy on its training data but only 60% accuracy on new orders. Which term describes this problem?

options.why: An underfit model does badly even on its training data because it never found the pattern. This model does very well on training data.
Overfitting is when a model gives accurate predictions for training data but not for real-world data. It memorised the practice questions instead of learning the subject.
Labeling is tagging training data with correct answers. It isn't a name for the gap between training and real-world results.
Batch inference is a way to run predictions over many records at once. It doesn't explain why the predictions are worse on new data.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'great on training data, poor on new data'. Rule: overfit = memorised (high variance); underfit = never learned (high bias).

questions.stem: A lender has 10 years of past loan applications, and each record is marked 'repaid' or 'defaulted'. It wants a model that predicts which new applicants will default. Which type of machine learning fits?

options.why: Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns in unlabeled data. This data already has the answer attached to every record.
Reinforcement learning learns by trial and error from rewards in an environment. The lender has historical records with known outcomes instead.
Self-supervised learning is how foundation models learn from huge amounts of data without human labels. Here the labels already exist and the task is narrow.
Supervised learning trains on input data paired with labeled outputs, here 'repaid' or 'defaulted', and learns to predict the label for new cases.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'each record is marked'. Rule: labeled data = supervised; no labels = unsupervised; rewards = reinforcement.

questions.stem: A research team has 5 million network log entries. None of them are tagged, and the team wants a model to discover hidden patterns in the data on its own. Which type of machine learning should it use?

options.why: Unsupervised learning trains a model to discover hidden patterns in unlabeled data, which is exactly this situation.
Supervised learning needs each example paired with a correct answer. These log entries have no tags.
Reinforcement learning needs an agent taking actions and receiving rewards. Here there is only a pile of existing data to explore.
Regression is a supervised technique that predicts a number from labeled examples. There is no labeled number to predict.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'none of them are tagged' + 'discover patterns'. Rule: no labels = unsupervised.

questions.stem: A logistics company wants software that learns the best route for warehouse robots by trying moves, getting points for fast deliveries, and losing points for collisions. Which type of machine learning is this?

options.why: Supervised learning learns from a fixed set of labeled examples. Here the software learns from the results of its own actions.
Unsupervised learning finds groups or patterns in unlabeled data. It has no rewards or penalties for actions.
Reinforcement learning trains an agent to make decisions by trial and error, maximising a reward. Points for speed and penalties for collisions are that reward.
Clustering groups similar data points together. It doesn't learn a sequence of actions from rewards.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'trying moves' + 'points' + 'penalties'. Rule: reward and trial-and-error = reinforcement learning.

questions.stem: A data analyst is sorting a utility company's data sources by type. Which pairing of data source and data type is correct?

options.text: Smart-meter readings recorded every 15 minutes for two years → time-series data
options.why: Time-series data is a sequence of values recorded in time order, which is what regular meter readings are.

options.text: Recorded customer phone calls → structured data
options.why: Audio doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns, so call recordings are unstructured data.

options.text: A table of customer IDs, addresses and bill amounts → unstructured data
options.why: Numbers, short text and dates in a table are the textbook example of structured, tabular data.

options.text: Photos of damaged power lines → tabular data
options.why: Photos are image data, which is unstructured. Tabular data lives in rows and columns.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'every 15 minutes'. Rule: ordered by time = time-series; rows and columns = structured/tabular; audio, images, long text = unstructured.

questions.stem: An insurance company is listing the data it holds before starting an AI project. Which of these are examples of unstructured data? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: A spreadsheet of policy numbers, start dates and premiums
options.why: Numbers, short text and dates that fit neatly into a table are structured data.

options.text: Audio recordings of claims phone calls
options.why: Audio doesn't fit neatly into a data table, so it is unstructured data.

options.text: Dashcam video footage submitted with car claims
options.why: Video is a standard example of unstructured data because of its size and nature.

options.text: A database table of customer IDs and postcodes
options.why: A database table with fixed columns is structured data.

options.text: A CSV file of monthly claim totals by region
options.why: A CSV of numbers in rows and columns is structured, tabular data.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'unstructured'. Rule: if it fits in a spreadsheet, it's structured; audio, video, images and long documents are unstructured.

questions.stem: A ride-sharing app must show a fare estimate within a fraction of a second while the rider waits on screen. Which inference option in Amazon SageMaker AI fits this requirement?

options.why: Batch transform scores a large dataset in one go with no persistent endpoint. A rider waiting on screen can't wait for a batch job.
Asynchronous inference queues requests for large payloads and long processing. It is near real-time at best, not instant.
Real-time inference is ideal for interactive workloads with low latency requirements, like an on-screen fare estimate.
Serverless inference suits traffic with idle periods and can tolerate cold starts. A cold start could make the waiting rider wait longer.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'fraction of a second' + 'waits on screen'. Rule: interactive and low latency = real-time endpoint.

questions.stem: A hospital sends large medical scans, each several hundred megabytes, to a model that can take up to 20 minutes per scan. Results are needed soon but not instantly. Which Amazon SageMaker AI inference option fits BEST?

options.why: Real-time inference is built for fast, interactive responses. Very large payloads and long processing times are what the asynchronous option is for.
Asynchronous inference queues requests and is ideal for large payloads (up to 1 GB), long processing times (up to one hour) and near real-time latency.
Serverless inference is for spiky traffic with idle periods. It isn't the option designed for very large payloads and long processing.
Batch transform is for scoring a whole dataset when no one is waiting. Here each scan arrives on its own and results are wanted soon.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'large payload' + 'long processing' + 'soon but not instantly'. Rule: big and slow but still wanted soon = asynchronous.

questions.stem: An energy company wants to score its entire customer file of 3 million records once a week to predict who might switch suppliers. No one waits for individual results. Which inference option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: A real-time endpoint that runs all week
options.why: A real-time endpoint stays running and is paid for all week, even though it is only needed for one weekly job.
Asynchronous inference handles individual large requests that are wanted fairly soon. A weekly run over a whole file is a batch job.
Serverless inference is for unpredictable request-by-request traffic. It isn't the tool for scoring a whole dataset at once.
Batch transform gets inferences from large datasets when you don't need a persistent endpoint, so nothing sits idle between weekly runs.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'entire file' + 'once a week' + 'no one waits'. Rule: whole dataset on a schedule = batch.

questions.stem: A small online shop gets a few bursts of prediction requests during the day and long quiet periods in between. It can accept an occasional short delay and doesn't want to manage any infrastructure. Which Amazon SageMaker AI inference option fits BEST?

options.why: Serverless inference needs no infrastructure management and is ideal for workloads with idle periods between traffic spurts that can tolerate cold starts.
A real-time endpoint keeps capacity running all day, including the long quiet periods the shop would pay for without using.
Batch transform scores a whole dataset in one job. The shop needs answers to individual requests as they arrive.
Asynchronous inference is designed for large payloads and long processing times. These are small, bursty requests.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'quiet periods' + 'occasional short delay' + 'no infrastructure'. Rule: spiky traffic that can tolerate cold starts = serverless.

questions.stem: A mortgage team wants an ML model to rank incoming applications by risk so its underwriters review the riskiest ones first. The underwriters still make the final decision. Which way that AI adds value does this describe?

options.text: Guaranteeing an exact, rule-based outcome for every applicant
options.why: ML gives predictions, not guaranteed outcomes. When an exact outcome is required, ML is the wrong tool.
The model ranks the work and people make the call. That is AI helping humans decide, not replacing them.

options.text: Removing the need for any historical data
options.why: An ML model needs historical data to learn from. This benefit doesn't exist.

options.text: Replacing the underwriters with fully automated approval
options.why: The scenario says the underwriters still make the final decision, so nothing is fully automated.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'underwriters still make the final decision'. Rule: AI ranks, flags or suggests and a person decides = assisting human decision making.

questions.stem: A payroll company must calculate each employee's tax using fixed rates set by law. Every result must be exactly correct and match the published rules. Which approach should the company use?

options.text: Train a supervised ML model on past payslips to predict the tax
options.why: An ML model gives a prediction that is usually close. The law requires the exact figure, which a prediction can't guarantee.

options.text: Use a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock to work out the tax for each payslip
options.why: A generative model can produce inaccurate answers and may vary between runs. Exact legal calculations need fixed rules.

options.text: A rules-based program that applies the published tax rates
options.why: When a specific outcome is needed instead of a prediction, ML is not appropriate. Writing the published rules into ordinary software is cheaper and always exact.

options.text: Use clustering to group employees and apply an average tax per group
options.why: Clustering finds similar groups in data. An average per group would be wrong for most individual employees.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'fixed rates' + 'exactly correct'. Rule: if the rules are known and the answer must be exact, write the rules; don't predict.

questions.stem: A family-run hardware store stocks 300 items and reorders each item when it drops below a set level. The owner asks whether to build an ML model for inventory. What is the BEST recommendation based on cost-benefit analysis?

options.text: Train a custom deep learning model on Amazon SageMaker AI
options.why: Deep learning needs lots of data, compute and ongoing maintenance. A simple reorder rule already works, so the cost isn't justified.

options.text: Use reinforcement learning to discover the best reorder levels
options.why: Reinforcement learning needs many trial-and-error runs to learn. That is a large investment for a problem simple rules already solve.

options.text: Keep a simple rules-based reorder system
options.why: ML needs real investment in data, hardware and upkeep that must be justified by business value. AWS gives simple inventory management as an example better served by rules.

options.text: Replace the reorder rule with a large language model
options.why: An LLM is built for language tasks, adds per-use cost, and can give inaccurate answers. None of that helps a fixed reorder threshold.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'set level' + 'small shop'. Rule: when a cheap rule already works, ML must beat the rule by more than it costs.

questions.stem: A real estate website wants to predict the selling price in dollars of each home from its size, location and age, using past sales. Which ML technique should it use?

options.why: Classification predicts a category, such as 'will sell' or 'won't sell'. A price in dollars is a continuous number.
Clustering groups similar homes without labels. It doesn't predict a specific price.
Reinforcement learning learns actions from rewards. Predicting a price from past sales is a supervised problem.
Regression is supervised learning that predicts a continuous value, such as a price.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'price in dollars'. Rule: a number = regression; a category = classification; groups with no labels = clustering.

questions.stem: A telecom company is reviewing ideas for ML projects. Which of these are classification problems? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Predicting whether each customer will cancel next month: yes or no
options.why: Yes or no is a category, so this is classification (binary classification).

options.text: Predicting next quarter's total revenue in dollars
options.why: A dollar amount is a continuous number, so this is regression.
Choosing one of several labeled categories is classification (multi-class classification).

options.text: Grouping customers into segments nobody has defined yet
options.why: Finding groups with no labels is clustering, an unsupervised technique.

options.text: Estimating how many minutes each call will last
options.why: Minutes are a continuous number, so this is regression.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'yes or no' and a fixed list of categories. Rule: pick-a-label = classification; how-much or how-many = regression.

questions.stem: A clothing retailer wants to split its shoppers into groups with similar buying habits for marketing. It has no existing labels for these groups. Which ML technique should it use?

options.why: Clustering is an unsupervised technique that groups similar data points together without needing labels.
Classification needs labeled examples of each group to learn from. The retailer has no labels.
Regression predicts a number, such as spend next month. It doesn't create groups.
Reinforcement learning learns actions from rewards. Segmenting shoppers is about finding groups in existing data.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'groups' + 'no existing labels'. Rule: find the groups yourself = clustering; sort into known groups = classification.

questions.stem: A bank's operations lead is deciding which problems deserve ML rather than fixed rules. Which problems are the BEST fit for ML? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Detecting card fraud, where criminals keep changing their tactics
options.why: AWS gives fraud detection as a problem that benefits from ML because fraudulent behavior keeps evolving, and hand-written rules can't keep up.

options.text: Applying a fixed $5 fee to every late payment
options.why: A fixed fee is an exact rule. A simple if-statement is cheaper and always right.

options.text: Forecasting next month's cash withdrawals at each ATM from years of history
options.why: Forecasting from historical patterns is a classic ML use case. No simple rule captures seasons, holidays and local trends.

options.text: Rounding interest to two decimal places
options.why: Rounding follows a precise rule with one correct answer. ML would add cost and risk for no benefit.

options.text: Blocking logins after five wrong passwords
options.why: This is a fixed threshold policy. A rule does it exactly; a prediction would only get it roughly right.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'keep changing' and 'from years of history'. Rule: patterns too messy or changing for rules = ML; known exact rules = code.

questions.stem: A consultant is matching business problems to real-world AI applications for a client workshop. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Suggesting films a viewer may like based on what they watched → speech recognition
options.why: Suggesting items from past behavior is a recommendation system. Speech recognition turns audio into text.

options.text: Turning recorded doctor dictation into typed notes → speech recognition
options.why: Converting spoken audio into text is exactly what speech recognition does.

options.text: Spotting unsafe images uploaded to a forum → natural language processing
options.why: Images are visual input, so this is computer vision, not language processing.

options.text: Predicting next month's product demand → computer vision
options.why: Predicting future demand from past numbers is forecasting. Computer vision works with images and video.

questions.trap: Key hint: the input type. Rule: audio in = speech recognition; images in = computer vision; past behavior in, suggestions out = recommendations; numbers over time = forecasting.

questions.stem: A call center wants to convert thousands of recorded customer calls into text so supervisors can search them. Which AWS service should it use?

options.why: Polly goes the other way: it turns text into lifelike speech.
Translate converts text from one language to another. It doesn't turn audio into text.
Comprehend finds insights like sentiment in text that already exists. The calls must first become text.
Transcribe is an automatic speech recognition service that converts audio to text, in real time or in batch.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'recorded calls' + 'into text'. Rule: Transcribe hears (speech to text); Polly speaks (text to speech).

questions.stem: An online store writes its product descriptions in English and wants them available in Spanish, French and Japanese without hiring translators. Which AWS service should it use?

options.why: Comprehend can detect which language a text is in, but it doesn't translate it.
Translate is a text translation service that uses machine learning to provide high-quality translation on demand.
Transcribe turns speech into text. The descriptions are already text.
Lex builds chatbots and voice interfaces. It isn't a service for translating documents.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'in Spanish, French and Japanese'. Rule: text in one language to text in another = Translate.

questions.stem: A restaurant chain collects thousands of written reviews each week and wants to know which ones are positive, negative or neutral, with the LEAST effort and no ML expertise. Which AWS service should it use?

options.why: Comprehend uses natural language processing to extract insights from text, including sentiment, with a ready-made pre-trained model.
Rekognition analyzes images and video. Reviews are text.
SageMaker AI could train a custom sentiment model, but that takes ML expertise and far more effort than a pre-trained service.
Polly reads text aloud as speech. It doesn't judge whether text is positive or negative.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'sentiment' + 'least effort'. Rule: insights from text (sentiment, entities, key phrases, PII) = Comprehend.

questions.stem: A pizza company wants customers to place orders through a chatbot on its website and by talking to its phone line. Which AWS service is designed to build these conversational interfaces?

options.why: Polly can give the bot a voice, but it only turns text into speech. It doesn't understand what the customer wants.
Transcribe turns speech into text, but it doesn't manage a conversation or work out the customer's intent.
Lex builds conversational interfaces using voice and text, with natural language understanding and automatic speech recognition built in.
Personalize recommends items to users. It doesn't run a conversation.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'chatbot' + 'voice and text'. Rule: build a conversational bot = Lex.

questions.stem: A news website wants to offer an audio version of every article so visually impaired readers can listen to it. Which AWS service should it use?

options.why: Transcribe does the reverse: it turns audio into text.
Polly converts text into lifelike speech, which is exactly an audio version of a written article.
Translate changes the language of text. It doesn't produce audio.
Textract extracts text and tables from scanned documents. It doesn't create speech.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'audio version' of text. Rule: Polly = parrot, it speaks text aloud.

questions.stem: A software company wants to find out how customers feel during support calls. It has only the audio recordings. Which AWS services should it combine? (Choose TWO.)

options.why: Transcribe first converts the call audio into text, which the sentiment step needs.
Comprehend then reads the transcripts and finds the sentiment in them.
Polly turns text into speech. The company already has speech and needs text.
Lex builds chatbots that talk with customers. It isn't used to analyze calls that already happened.
Translate changes the language of text. Nothing in the scenario says the calls need translating.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'how customers feel' + 'audio recordings'. Rule: audio to text with Transcribe, then text to sentiment with Comprehend.

questions.stem: A trainer is building a cheat sheet of AWS AI services. Which pairing of service and capability is correct?

options.text: Amazon Transcribe → turns written text into lifelike speech
options.why: That is Polly. Transcribe turns speech into text.

options.text: Amazon Lex → translates documents between languages
options.why: That is Translate. Lex builds conversational chatbots.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend → finds objects and faces in photos
options.why: That is Rekognition. Comprehend works on text.

options.text: Amazon Textract → pulls typed and handwritten text, forms and tables from scanned documents
options.why: Textract detects typed and handwritten text and extracts text, forms and tables from documents.

questions.trap: Key hint: the verb in each pairing. Rule: Transcribe hears, Polly speaks, Translate converts language, Comprehend reads meaning, Lex chats, Rekognition sees, Textract reads documents.

questions.stem: A photo-sharing app wants to automatically detect unsafe or inappropriate images before they are published, without training its own model. Which AWS service should it use?

options.why: Comprehend analyzes text, not images.
Textract pulls text and tables out of documents. It doesn't judge whether a photo is unsafe.
Rekognition is a pre-trained image and video analysis service, and detecting unsafe content is one of its built-in features.
Personalize recommends items to users. It doesn't inspect image content.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'images' + 'unsafe'. Rule: pictures or video, pre-trained = Rekognition.

questions.stem: An online bookstore wants to show each shopper 'books you might like' based on their browsing and purchase history, using a fully managed service. Which AWS service should it use?

options.why: Personalize is a fully managed ML service that uses your data to generate item recommendations for your users.
Comprehend finds insights in text, such as sentiment. It doesn't generate product recommendations.
Lex builds chatbots. A chatbot could talk about books, but it doesn't learn what each shopper likes from their history.
Translate converts text between languages. It has nothing to do with recommendations.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'you might like' + 'purchase history'. Rule: recommendations = Personalize.

questions.stem: A regulated lender must explain to regulators and to each rejected applicant which factors led to a credit decision. It has years of labeled, tabular loan data. Which approach fits BEST?

options.text: Ask a large foundation model to approve or reject each application from a written summary
options.why: Foundation models are often seen as black boxes and can vary their answers. That makes it hard to give regulators a reliable reason for each decision.

options.text: Train a traditional supervised ML model on the labeled loan data, chosen so its predictions can be explained
options.why: With labeled tabular data and a strict explainability requirement, a traditional ML model is the better fit. Its predictions are easier to explain and audit.

options.text: Use an unsupervised clustering model to group applicants
options.why: Clustering finds groups without labels. It doesn't make approve-or-reject decisions and ignores the labeled history.

options.text: Generate a different explanation for each applicant with a text-generation model after the decision is made
options.why: A generated explanation may sound convincing but isn't guaranteed to reflect how the decision was made, and it could be a hallucination.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'regulators' + 'explain which factors'. Rule: regulation and explainability requirements point to traditional ML; open-ended content points to foundation models.

questions.stem: A company is deciding between a traditional ML model and a foundation model (FM) for several projects. Which tasks are better suited to an FM? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Summarizing long customer emails into three bullet points
options.why: Summarization is a core generative AI use case. An FM can do it from a prompt with no labeled training data.

options.text: Drafting first versions of product descriptions in the brand's tone
options.why: Generating new text content is what foundation models are built for.

options.text: Scoring millions of sensor readings per second for faults on a tight budget
options.why: Large FMs are slower and costlier to run. High-volume, low-latency numeric scoring is an operational constraint that favors a small traditional model.

options.text: Making credit decisions that must be explained factor by factor to a regulator
options.why: Strict explainability and regulatory requirements favor traditional ML, whose decisions are easier to explain.

options.text: Predicting a house price from ten numeric columns
options.why: This is a standard regression problem on tabular data. A traditional ML model is cheaper and easier to explain.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'summarizing' and 'drafting'. Rule: create or rewrite content = FM; explainable, cheap, fast numeric prediction = traditional ML.

questions.stem: A new analyst is learning the phases of the ML lifecycle described in the AWS Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Data processing → business goal identification → model deployment → ML problem framing → model development → model monitoring
options.why: Processing data before knowing the business goal means you don't yet know which data matters. The goal always comes first.

options.text: Business goal identification → ML problem framing → data processing → model development → model deployment → model monitoring
options.why: This is the lens's order: know the goal, frame it as an ML problem, prepare the data, build the model, deploy it, then keep monitoring it.

options.text: ML problem framing → model development → data processing → business goal identification → model monitoring → model deployment
options.why: A model can't be developed before its data is prepared, and it can't be monitored before it is deployed.

options.text: Model development → model deployment → business goal identification → data processing → ML problem framing → model monitoring
options.why: Building a model first and asking what the business wants afterwards is the classic way ML projects fail.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'sequence'. Rule: goal, frame, data, develop, deploy, monitor, with feedback loops back to earlier phases.

questions.stem: A retailer's demand model has been in production for six months, and its predictions are getting worse. Which checks belong to the model monitoring component of an ML pipeline? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Comparing live input data with the data the model was trained on
options.why: Data quality monitoring compares live data to training data to catch drift, such as shoppers behaving differently from last year.

options.text: Comparing the model's predictions with the actual outcomes once they are known
options.why: Model quality monitoring compares predictions with the actual ground truth labels to see whether accuracy is slipping.

options.text: Writing the business goal for the project
options.why: Setting the business goal is the first lifecycle phase, not monitoring a model already in production.

options.text: Choosing which algorithm to train first
options.why: Picking an algorithm is part of model development, which happens before deployment.
Data collection is part of data processing, early in the lifecycle.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'in production' + 'getting worse'. Rule: monitoring watches live data against training data, and predictions against reality, then triggers retraining.

questions.stem: A startup wants to begin with an existing pre-trained, open-source model and adjust it for its task, instead of training a model from scratch. Which AWS option provides a hub of these models?

options.why: JumpStart is a machine learning hub that provides pretrained, open-source models for many problem types, which can be trained further and tuned before deployment.
Canvas is a no-code visual interface for building predictions from your own data. It isn't a hub of pre-trained open-source models.
Comprehend is a finished NLP service. You call it; you don't browse and adapt open-source models in it.
Amazon Quick is an AI-powered service for business analysis, automation and research. It isn't a model hub.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'pre-trained, open-source' + 'hub'. Rule: model hub inside SageMaker AI = JumpStart.

questions.stem: A shipping company has years of its own labeled data on package damage, and no pre-trained model covers its specific problem. Its data science team wants to build, train and deploy its own model on a fully managed service. Which AWS service fits?

options.why: Rekognition offers pre-trained image analysis. It doesn't give a data science team a full environment to build and train its own model from tabular damage data.
Personalize is only for recommendations. Predicting package damage isn't a recommendation problem.
SageMaker AI is a fully managed ML service for building, training and deploying your own models into a production-ready hosted environment.
Kiro is an agentic coding service that turns prompts into specs and code. It isn't the service that trains and hosts ML models.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'its own labeled data' + 'build, train and deploy'. Rule: training a custom model = SageMaker AI.

questions.stem: A marketing agency wants to add a foundation model to its app. It has no ML engineers and wants the LEAST operational overhead. How should it use the model in production?

options.text: Download an open-source model and host it on Amazon EC2 instances it manages
options.why: Self-hosting means the agency deploys, patches and scales the servers itself, which is the most operational overhead.

options.text: Train its own foundation model from scratch
options.why: Pre-training from scratch needs huge datasets and GPU clusters running for weeks. It is the opposite of low overhead.

options.text: Run the model on containers in Amazon EKS
options.why: EKS still requires the agency to package, deploy and operate the model itself.

options.text: Call the model through a managed API service such as Amazon Bedrock
options.why: A managed API service runs the model for you. Amazon Bedrock gives fully managed access to foundation models, so there is no infrastructure to operate.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'no ML engineers' + 'least operational overhead'. Rule: managed API = someone else runs the model; self-hosted = you run it.

questions.stem: A defense contractor must run a specific open-source model on compute that its own team deploys and manages end to end, including the servers and the API in front of them. Which production approach does this describe?

options.why: With a managed API service the provider runs the model and its infrastructure, which is what the contractor doesn't want.
Self-hosted models are deployed and managed by the organization using them, so the contractor's team controls the servers and the API.
Batch transform is a way of scoring a dataset in one job. It doesn't say who manages the infrastructure.

options.text: A pre-trained AI service such as Amazon Comprehend
options.why: Comprehend is a fully managed AWS service with its own models. The contractor can't bring its chosen open-source model to it.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'its own team deploys and manages'. Rule: you run the servers = self-hosted; AWS runs them = managed API.

questions.stem: A sales director with no coding skills wants interactive dashboards of her team's data and an AI assistant that can research questions and automate routine tasks. Which AWS service fits BEST?

options.why: SageMaker AI is for data scientists who build, train and deploy ML models. It isn't a business dashboard tool.
Kiro helps developers turn prompts into specs, code and tests. The director doesn't code.
Amazon Quick is an AI-powered service for analyzing data, automating tasks and conducting research, and it includes Quick Sight for interactive dashboards.
Transcribe turns speech into text. It doesn't build dashboards or research questions.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'dashboards' + 'no coding' + 'research'. Rule: business users analyzing and automating = Amazon Quick (it grew out of QuickSight).

questions.stem: A development team wants an AI tool that turns a plain-English feature request into a detailed spec and then into working code, documentation and tests. Which AWS service fits?

options.why: Kiro is an agentic coding service that turns prompts into detailed specs, then into working code, docs and tests.
Amazon Quick serves business users with analysis, research and automation. It isn't a coding tool for developers.
JumpStart is a hub of pre-trained ML models. It doesn't write application code from a spec.
Lex builds chatbots for customers. It doesn't generate specs and code.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'spec' + 'code' + 'tests'. Rule: agentic coding from specs = Kiro.

questions.stem: A business analyst who can't write code wants to build a model that forecasts weekly sales from a spreadsheet of past sales, using a visual interface. Which AWS option fits BEST?

options.why: Bedrock gives access to foundation models for generative AI. A numeric sales forecast from a spreadsheet is a traditional ML task.
Translate converts text between languages. It doesn't forecast anything.
Kiro is a coding tool for developers. The analyst wants a no-code visual interface.
SageMaker Canvas, part of SageMaker AI, lets you build ML models and generate predictions through a visual interface with no code, and it supports time-series forecasting.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'can't write code' + 'visual interface' + 'forecast'. Rule: no-code ML predictions = SageMaker Canvas.

questions.stem: An AI lead is mapping AWS services to the work each one supports. Which pairing of service and use is correct?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock → training a custom fraud model from scratch on labeled tabular data
options.why: Bedrock gives managed access to foundation models. Building and training a custom tabular model is SageMaker AI's job.

options.text: Amazon Quick → building, training and hosting custom ML models
options.why: Amazon Quick is for business analysis, research and automation. Building and hosting models is SageMaker AI.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock → building a generative AI app on foundation models from several providers through one API
options.why: Bedrock is a fully managed service that gives access to foundation models from many providers for building generative AI apps.

options.text: Kiro → dashboards and business intelligence for executives
options.why: Dashboards and BI are Amazon Quick. Kiro is for developers writing code from specs.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'generative AI app' + 'foundation models'. Rule: Bedrock = use FMs; SageMaker AI = build your own; Quick = business users; Kiro = developers.

questions.stem: A company's data scientists deploy models by hand from their laptops, and nobody can reproduce last year's model. Which MLOps practices would fix this? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Versioning data, code and models so every training run can be reproduced
options.why: MLOps uses versioning to make training reproducible and auditable, so last year's model can be rebuilt.

options.text: Automating training and deployment in a repeatable pipeline
options.why: MLOps automates workflows to ensure repeatability, consistency and scalability, replacing hand deployments from laptops.

options.text: Letting each data scientist choose their own deployment steps
options.why: That creates more one-off processes and more technical debt. MLOps aims for the same repeatable process every time.

options.text: Deleting old models once a new one is deployed
options.why: Throwing away old versions makes results impossible to reproduce or audit, which is the problem being solved.

options.text: Retraining models only when a customer complains
options.why: MLOps uses continuous monitoring and retraining so problems are caught early, not after customers notice.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'by hand' + 'can't reproduce'. Rule: MLOps = version everything, automate everything, monitor and retrain continuously.

questions.stem: An ML team wants to automate its end-to-end workflow, from data preparation through training to deployment, so it runs the same way every time. Which Amazon SageMaker AI feature should it use?

options.why: Canvas is a no-code interface for building predictions. It isn't a tool for automating a team's end-to-end workflow.
SageMaker Pipelines creates end-to-end machine learning workflows with purpose-built CI/CD tools, which makes the process repeatable.
JumpStart is a hub of pre-trained models. It gives you a starting model, not an automated workflow.
Polly turns text into speech. It plays no part in automating ML workflows.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'automate end-to-end workflow' + 'same way every time'. Rule: repeatable ML workflow = SageMaker Pipelines.

questions.stem: A bank must keep a catalog of every model version it has trained, see each version's lineage, and record which version was approved for production. Which Amazon SageMaker AI feature is designed for this?

options.why: Pipelines automates the workflow that produces models. The catalog of versions and their approval status lives in Model Registry.
Canvas lets non-coders build predictions. It isn't a governed catalog of model versions.
Model Registry catalogs models for production, manages model versions, shows model lineage and manages each model's approval status.
JumpStart is a hub of pre-trained models to start from. It doesn't track your own versions and approvals.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'every version' + 'approved for production'. Rule: versions and approvals = Model Registry; automated workflow = Pipelines.

questions.stem: A hospital's screening model looks at 1,000 scans, and 50 of the patients really have the disease. Missing a sick patient is far worse than a false alarm. Which metric should the hospital focus on MOST?

options.why: Precision asks: of the scans the model flagged, how many were really sick? It matters most when false alarms are costly, which isn't the worry here.
With only 50 sick patients out of 1,000, a model that calls everyone healthy scores 95% accuracy while missing every sick patient.
Recall asks: of the 50 truly sick patients, how many did the model find? AWS gives cancer testing as the classic case where recall matters, because the goal is to find all the true positives.
Cost per user is a business metric. It doesn't measure how many sick patients the model misses.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'missing a sick patient is far worse'. Rule: can't afford to miss one = recall; can't afford a false alarm = precision.

questions.stem: An email provider's spam filter moved 200 emails to the spam folder, and 190 of them really were spam. Users are angry whenever a real email is hidden as spam. Which metric does '190 of 200' measure?

options.why: Precision is how many of the items the model flagged were really positive: 190 of 200, or 95%. It matters when a false positive, like hiding a real email, is costly.
Recall would ask how many of all the spam emails that arrived were caught. The 200 flagged emails don't tell you that.
F1 combines precision and recall into one number. The '190 of 200' figure on its own is precision only.
ROI is a business metric about money. It doesn't count correct spam flags.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'of the 200 it flagged'. Rule: precision starts from what the model flagged; recall starts from what was really there.

questions.stem: A payments company's fraud model shows 99% accuracy, but only 1% of transactions are fraud. The company wants a single metric that balances catching fraud with avoiding false alarms. Which metric should it use?

options.why: When only 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that never flags anything is 99% accurate and useless. Accuracy hides that.
Precision only looks at false alarms. On its own it ignores how much fraud slips through.
Recall only looks at how much fraud is caught. On its own it ignores false alarms.
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it balances catching fraud with avoiding false alarms in one number.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'balances' + rare positives. Rule: accuracy lies on imbalanced data; F1 = one number that balances precision and recall.

questions.stem: A retailer's leadership team wants to know whether its new AI product-recommendation feature was worth building. Which are business metrics rather than model metrics? (Choose TWO.)

options.why: ROI compares the money the feature brings in or saves with what it cost, which is a business measure.
Cost per user measures what the feature costs to serve each customer, which is a business measure.
Precision measures how many of the model's positive predictions were right. It is a model metric.
Recall measures how many of the real positives the model found. It is a model metric.
F1 combines precision and recall. It describes the model, not the business result.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'worth building'. Rule: model metrics ask 'is it right?'; business metrics (ROI, cost per user, development cost, customer feedback) ask 'is it worth it?'.

questions.stem: A support team's generative AI bill is calculated per token. Which description of a token is correct?

options.text: Exactly one character of text, so a 10-letter word is always 10 tokens
options.why: Tokens are usually bigger than one character. Common words and phrases are often a single token.

options.text: A unit of text the model reads or writes, such as a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark
options.why: A token can be a whole word, a piece like "-ed", or a mark like "?". Models count and bill text in these units.

options.text: One complete sentence, however long it is
options.why: A sentence is normally split into many tokens, so billing per sentence would hide most of the cost.

options.text: The access key the application uses to call the model
options.why: That's a credential, not a unit of text. The "token" on a model bill measures how much text went in and out.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'billed per token'. Rule: a token is a chunk of text, roughly a word or a piece of one.

questions.stem: An outdoor retailer wants a search for "warm winter jacket" to also return a product described only as an "insulated parka". What should the search compare?

options.text: Exact keyword matches between the query and the description
options.why: Keyword matching needs shared words. "Jacket" and "parka" share none, so the product would be missed.

options.text: The number of tokens in each product description
options.why: Token count measures length, not meaning. Two unrelated texts can have the same count.

options.text: Embeddings: number vectors that place texts with similar meanings close together
options.why: Embeddings turn text into vectors, and similar meanings land near each other even when no words match.

options.text: The chunk size used to split the product catalog
options.why: Chunking decides how documents are cut up. It doesn't judge whether two texts mean the same thing.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'similar meaning, different words'. Rule: meaning-based search means embeddings and vectors.

questions.stem: A law firm's contracts are hundreds of pages long, far more than a model can read at one time. Which step breaks each contract into smaller pieces before the pieces are turned into embeddings?

options.why: Tokenization cuts text into word-sized units for the model. It doesn't produce passage-sized pieces for retrieval.
Fine-tuning retrains the model's weights on labeled examples. It doesn't split documents.
Distillation trains a small model from a large one. It has nothing to do with preparing documents.
Chunking splits large files into small pieces so each one fits in the model's context window.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'too long' + 'smaller pieces'. Rule: chunking cuts documents into passages; tokenization cuts text into word pieces.

questions.stem: A design agency needs a model that creates new images from text descriptions by starting with random noise and refining it step by step. Which type of model does this describe?

options.why: Diffusion models create data by making controlled random changes to a starting sample, over and over, until an image emerges.

options.text: A transformer-based large language model that only outputs text
options.why: A text-only language model writes words, not pictures.
Embedding models turn inputs into vectors for comparison. They don't generate new images.
Regression predicts a number, such as a price. It can't draw anything.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'starts from noise, refines step by step'. Rule: images from noise → diffusion model.

questions.stem: An insurer wants one model that accepts a photo of a damaged car together with the driver's written description, then drafts a claim summary. Which kind of model fits?

options.why: Diffusion models mainly generate images. The insurer needs a model that understands an image and writes text.
Multimodal models take in more than one type of data, such as images and text together.
A text-only model can read the description but can't look at the photo.
Clustering groups similar records. It can't read a photo and write a summary.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'photo together with text'. Rule: more than one data type in → multimodal model.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes a foundation model?

options.text: A small model trained on one company's labeled data to do a single task
options.why: That's a traditional task-specific ML model. A foundation model is general-purpose.

options.text: A database that stores embeddings for fast similarity search
options.why: That's a vector store. It holds vectors; it doesn't generate answers.

options.text: A large model pre-trained on a broad range of data that can be adapted to many different tasks
options.why: Foundation models have many parameters, learn from massive and varied data, and serve as a starting point for lots of jobs.

options.text: A set of hand-written if-then rules for a business process
options.why: Rules are written by people, not learned from data. That's not a model of any kind here.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'broad data' + 'many tasks'. Rule: foundation model = big, general, pre-trained, adaptable.

questions.stem: A product manager is learning how embeddings work. Which statements about embeddings are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: They are short human-readable summaries of each document.
options.why: Embeddings are numbers, not prose. A person can't read meaning straight out of them.

options.text: They permanently change the foundation model's weights.
options.why: Creating an embedding reads data through a model. It doesn't retrain that model.

options.text: They can only be created from text, never from images.
options.why: Images and other objects can be embedded too. Embeddings aren't limited to text.

options.text: Items with similar meanings end up with vectors that are close together.
options.why: That closeness is what makes embeddings useful for similarity search.

options.text: They represent text, images or other objects as lists of numbers called vectors.
options.why: Embeddings are numerical representations of real-world objects, stored as vectors.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'numbers' + 'similar'. Rule: embedding = meaning as a vector; close vectors = similar meaning.

questions.stem: A marketing analyst gets vague answers from a model. She rewrites her request to state the audience, the format and the length she wants, and the answers improve. The model itself was not changed. What is she doing?

options.why: Prompt engineering improves results by changing the instructions and context you send, with no change to the model.
Continued pre-training feeds the model large amounts of new unlabeled data. That's a training job, not a rewrite.
Fine-tuning retrains the model on labeled examples and changes its weights. She only changed her wording.
Chunking splits long documents into pieces. She rewrote a request instead.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'rewrote the request' + 'model not changed'. Rule: change the words → prompt engineering; change the weights → fine-tuning.

questions.stem: A team pastes a 900-page manual and a question into a model, and the request fails because the input is too long for the model to consider at once. Which limit did they hit?

options.why: Temperature controls how random the output is. It doesn't limit input size.
The context window is how much text, in tokens, a model can consider at one time.
Embedding size describes how long each vector is. It isn't what rejects a long prompt.
Maximum output tokens caps how long the answer can be. The problem here is the size of the input.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'too long to consider at once'. Rule: input too big → context window; answer too long → max tokens.

questions.stem: A contact center records hour-long calls. Supervisors want a short paragraph for each call that captures the customer's problem and the outcome. Which generative AI use case fits BEST?

options.why: Recommendations suggest items a user might like. Nobody here wants suggestions.
Translation changes the language, not the length. The calls need shortening, not converting.
Summarization condenses long content into its key points, which is exactly what supervisors want.
The input and output here are text. No pictures are needed.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'hour-long' → 'short paragraph'. Rule: long in, short out, same meaning = summarization.

questions.stem: A retailer is choosing where to try generative AI first. Which tasks are good fits for generative AI? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Applying a fixed rule that any order over $500 needs manager approval
options.why: A known rule is a simple if-statement. Using AI for it adds cost and risk for no gain.

options.text: Generating starter code from a plain-English description of a small script
options.why: Code generation is one of the named generative AI use cases.

options.text: Drafting first versions of product descriptions for a catalog
options.why: Creating new text from a few facts is a core generative AI strength.

options.text: Recording every sale in the accounting ledger
options.why: Recording data is a database job. Nothing needs to be generated.

options.text: Calculating each employee's payroll tax to the exact cent
options.why: Payroll needs the same exact answer every time. A fixed calculation beats a model that can vary or be wrong.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'drafting' and 'generating'. Rule: create new content → generative AI; exact, rule-bound answer → normal code.

questions.stem: Which pairing of business need and generative AI use case is correct?

options.text: A hotel chain wants its web chat to answer guest questions at any hour → AI assistant / customer service agent
options.why: A conversational assistant that answers questions around the clock is the customer service agent use case.

options.text: A news site wants articles available in Spanish → summarization
options.why: Changing the language of a text is translation, not summarization.

options.text: A streaming service wants to suggest shows each viewer might like → code generation
options.why: Suggesting shows is a recommendation engine. Code generation writes software.

options.text: A game studio wants concept art from a text description → recommendation engine
options.why: Creating art from a description is image generation. Recommendations suggest existing items.

questions.trap: Key hint: match the verb to the use case. Rule: answer → assistant, convert language → translation, make pictures → image generation, suggest → recommendations.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders these stages of the foundation model lifecycle?

options.why: Deploying before fine-tuning and testing puts an unfinished, untested model in front of users.
The model first learns broadly, is then specialised, is tested, goes live, and finally collects feedback for the next round.
Fine-tuning adjusts an already pre-trained model, so it can't come first. Evaluation should also happen before deployment.
You can't evaluate a model that hasn't been trained yet, and feedback comes from a model that's already live.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'order the lifecycle'. Rule: learn broadly, specialise, test, ship, listen.

questions.stem: After launching a writing assistant, a company collects thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings from real users to guide the next version. Which foundation model lifecycle stage is this?

options.why: Data selection picks what the model will train on. User ratings after launch come later.
Pre-training is the initial learning on massive data, long before any user sees the model.
Feedback is the stage after deployment where real-world use shapes the next improvement.
Evaluation tests the model before it's deployed, usually on benchmark datasets or with reviewers. These ratings come from live users after launch.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'after launching' + 'real users'. Rule: before launch = evaluation; after launch = feedback.

questions.stem: A startup builds its app on a foundation model from Amazon Bedrock. Which lifecycle stage did the model provider already complete, and is usually the most expensive in compute?

options.text: Collecting feedback from the startup's users
options.why: Only the startup can collect feedback from its own users.
Putting the model into the app is the startup's job, not the provider's.

options.text: Fine-tuning on the startup's own examples
options.why: Fine-tuning on the startup's data only happens if the startup chooses to do it, and it costs far less than pre-training.
Pre-training builds the model from scratch on massive data and needs GPU clusters running for weeks. The provider has already paid for it.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'already complete' + 'most expensive'. Rule: pre-training is the provider's weeks-of-GPUs step; you start after it.

questions.stem: A company uses on-demand inference on Amazon Bedrock. Its monthly bill doubled after it added a long policy document to the start of every prompt, though the number of requests stayed the same. What explains the increase?

options.text: On-demand pricing charges for the input and output tokens processed, so longer prompts cost more
options.why: Every token sent in is billed, so a long document on every request multiplies the input cost.

options.text: On-demand pricing charges a flat fee per request, so the document should not matter
options.why: On-demand isn't a flat per-request fee. The request count stayed the same and the bill still doubled, so length is what's billed.

options.text: Bedrock charges a storage fee for every document placed in a prompt
options.why: Prompts aren't billed as storage. The extra cost comes from the extra input tokens.

options.text: On-demand pricing charges per hour that the model is available
options.why: Hourly billing is Provisioned Throughput. On-demand charges for tokens.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'on-demand' + 'longer prompt'. Rule: on-demand = pay per input and output token.

questions.stem: A company wants to reduce its on-demand inference costs without changing the model. Which actions will help? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Set a maximum output length so responses aren't longer than needed
options.why: Output tokens are billed too, so capping response length cuts cost.

options.text: Raise the temperature so responses are more creative
options.why: Temperature changes how random the wording is. It doesn't reduce the number of tokens billed.

options.text: Remove unneeded text from the instructions sent with every request
options.why: Fewer input tokens per request means a smaller bill, because every input token is charged.

options.text: Paste the whole conversation history into every request, even when it isn't needed
options.why: Resending unneeded history adds input tokens and makes each call more expensive.

options.text: Add ten more worked examples to every prompt
options.why: Extra examples add input tokens to every request, so the bill goes up.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'reduce cost' + 'on-demand'. Rule: fewer tokens in, fewer tokens out, smaller bill.

questions.stem: A chatbot on Amazon Bedrock puts the same long product manual at the start of every on-demand request, followed by a short customer question. Which feature reduces the input token cost and the response latency for this pattern?

options.why: Batch suits large offline jobs, not live chat. Prompt caching also isn't supported with the batch inference API.
Provisioned Throughput buys fixed capacity by the hour. It doesn't stop you paying to resend the same manual.
Prompt caching reuses long, repeated context, cutting latency and input token costs. It works best with static content at the start of the prompt.
Temperature changes randomness, not cost or speed.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'same long content' + 'every request'. Rule: repeated static prefix → prompt caching.

questions.stem: A company compares two foundation models for a high-volume task that sorts short customer emails into five categories. Both models meet the accuracy target. Why would the smaller model usually be the better choice?

options.text: Smaller models have larger context windows
options.why: Context window size varies by model, not by being small. Short emails don't need a large window anyway.

options.text: Smaller models don't charge for input tokens
options.why: Token-priced models charge for input tokens whatever their size.
Any generative model can produce wrong output. Size doesn't remove that risk.

options.text: Smaller models generally cost less per request and respond faster
options.why: Price depends partly on model size, and larger models tend to be slower. When both are accurate enough, smaller saves money and time.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'high-volume' + 'both meet the target'. Rule: good enough and smaller = cheaper and faster.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes context engineering?

options.text: Designing the system that decides what information goes into the model's context window for each task, such as instructions, memory, retrieved documents and tool definitions
options.why: Context engineering focuses on what to show the model and assembles it dynamically for every request.

options.text: Retraining the model's weights on company documents
options.why: That's fine-tuning or continued pre-training. Context engineering changes what the model sees, not the model.

options.text: Rewording a single question until the model answers it well
options.why: That's prompt engineering, which focuses on what to ask. Context engineering covers everything else the model is shown.

options.text: Choosing the largest available model so it knows more
options.why: Model choice is a selection decision. It doesn't control the information each request carries.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'what the model is shown'. Rule: prompt engineering = what to ask; context engineering = what to show.

questions.stem: A team is applying context engineering to a banking assistant. Which items are they deciding whether to place in the model's context window? (Choose THREE.)

options.why: Weights are part of the model itself. They're never placed in a prompt.

options.text: Memory of the customer's earlier conversations
options.why: Memory is one of the named parts of a well-engineered context.

options.text: Definitions of the tools and MCP servers the assistant can call
options.why: Tool definitions and MCP servers are listed as context components, so the model knows what it can do.

options.text: Passages retrieved from a knowledge base
options.why: Knowledge base content is a standard context component, supplied at request time.

options.text: The number of training epochs used to build the model
options.why: Training settings belong to how the model was made, not to what it sees per request.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'context window' + 'deciding what to include'. Rule: context = instructions, query, profile, memory, tools and knowledge, never the weights.

questions.stem: A developer has polished the wording of an assistant's instructions, but it still can't answer "Where is my order?" because it never receives the customer's order history. Which practice addresses this gap?

options.text: Fine-tuning the model on last year's orders
options.why: Orders change constantly, and baking old ones into the weights would give stale answers.

options.text: Distilling the model into a smaller one
options.why: A smaller model would still lack the order history.

options.text: Context engineering, so the system pulls the customer's order history into each request
options.why: The problem is missing information, not wording. Context engineering decides what data reaches the model on each request.

options.text: More prompt engineering on the instruction wording
options.why: The wording is already polished. No phrasing can supply order data the model never sees.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'never receives' the data. Rule: missing facts at request time → context engineering, not better wording.

questions.stem: A company wants its AI agents to connect to many external tools and data sources through one open standard, instead of writing a custom integration for each system. What should it use?

options.why: Guardrails filter harmful content and sensitive data. They don't connect agents to tools.
Knowledge Bases handle retrieval from your documents. They aren't a general standard for connecting agents to any tool.
Prompt Management saves and versions prompts. It doesn't link agents to outside systems.
MCP is an open protocol that connects LLM applications to external tools and data. One standard replaces a custom integration per system.

questions.stem: What does a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server offer to an AI application?

options.text: A dashboard for business intelligence reports

options.text: Dedicated GPU capacity billed by the hour

options.text: The weights and training data of the foundation model
options.why: MCP connects apps to outside systems. It doesn't hand out model internals.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'MCP server'. Rule: MCP serves tools, resources and prompts.

questions.stem: A travel company's AI assistant must quote today's flight prices, which change by the minute. What capability lets the agent get these prices?

options.why: A bigger window holds more text, but someone still has to fetch today's prices.

options.why: Agents extend their abilities by invoking tools, and a live API is the only source of minute-by-minute prices.
Temperature changes how varied the wording is. It can't fetch data.

options.text: Fine-tuning the model on last month's flight prices
options.why: Training bakes in old prices. They'd be wrong by the time anyone asked.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'live' data that changes constantly. Rule: agent needs fresh facts or actions → tool use.

questions.stem: A shopping agent should remember each customer's shoe size and favourite brands across visits weeks apart. Which kind of agent memory does this need?

options.why: Temperature makes answers more predictable. It stores nothing.
The context window only covers the current request. It keeps nothing between visits.
Long-term memory holds knowledge that persists across sessions, so the agent recognises returning customers.
Short-term memory holds the state of the current conversation and is gone when the session ends.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'across visits'. Rule: this conversation → short-term; across sessions → long-term memory.

questions.stem: A supervisor agent receives a customer request, splits it into subtasks, hands them to separate billing, shipping and returns agents, and then combines their answers. Which multi-agent pattern is this?

options.text: A horizontal pattern of peer agents with no coordinator
options.why: In a horizontal pattern, peers collaborate side by side. Here one agent is clearly in charge.

options.text: A single agent using retrieval augmented generation
options.why: RAG fetches documents for one model. This request is split across several agents.
Batch inference runs many prompts offline at a lower price. It's a pricing mode, not an agent pattern.

options.text: A vertical (hierarchical) pattern with a supervisor delegating to subagents

questions.trap: Key hint: 'supervisor' + 'hands them to'. Rule: boss plus workers = vertical/hierarchical; equals working together = horizontal.

questions.stem: A research firm has a legal agent, a finance agent and a market agent that share findings directly with each other as equals to produce a joint report. No agent directs the others. Which multi-agent pattern is this?

options.why: Horizontal means lateral collaboration among specialised agents, with no one in charge.
Vertical needs a supervisor directing subagents. The stem says no agent directs the others.
There are three agents here, not one agent calling tools.
Chaining passes prompts through a single model. This describes separate agents.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'as equals' + 'no agent directs'. Rule: peers = horizontal; supervisor = vertical.

questions.stem: An insurer wants AI to handle a claim from start to finish. It must check the policy, request photos, estimate the cost and schedule a repair, coordinating several systems and subagents along the way. Which agentic concept covers managing this multistep process?

options.why: Chunking splits documents for retrieval. It doesn't run a process.
Workflow orchestration agents coordinate multistep tasks across systems and delegate work to subagents.
Distillation trains a smaller model from a larger one. It doesn't manage tasks.
Tokenization breaks text into model units. It doesn't coordinate anything.

questions.trap: Key hint: 'multistep' + 'coordinating systems'. Rule: many steps across many systems → workflow orchestration.

questions.stem: What BEST separates an AI agent from a basic chatbot that only answers questions?

options.text: The agent's answers are guaranteed to be correct
